opts: Choosing the passwords for each customer's staff
Classifying the data that each customer stores
Writing the application code for each customer
Logical isolation between the tenants' data
why: Multitenancy relies on the provider keeping tenants isolated from each other. Passwords, code and data classification belong to the customers.

q: A cloud audit finds a storage bucket that anyone can read and a database management port open to the whole internet. What do these findings represent?
why: Open buckets and exposed ports are settings the customer controls, and misconfiguration is among the most common causes of cloud exposure. Nothing here points to a hardware failure, a hypervisor flaw or a quantum threat.

q: Which two are recognized Bluetooth risks? (Choose two.)
opts: Bluesnarfing, the unauthorized copying of data from a device
Bluejacking, the sending of unsolicited messages
why: Bluetooth devices can suffer bluesnarfing and bluejacking when they are discoverable or poorly configured. The other three are attacks on DNS, web databases and network broadcast replies.

q: Which two practices improve the security of IoT devices? (Choose two.)
opts: Place the devices on a separate network segment
Leave default passwords so support can help
Expose the management page to the internet
Turn off logging to save space
why: Unique credentials and segmentation limit misuse and spread. Defaults, internet exposure and no logging all raise risk.

q: Which two statements about industrial control systems are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Safety and availability usually outrank confidentiality
Many devices run legacy software that is hard to patch
They are always isolated from every other network
They follow the same patching schedule as office laptops
why: Operational technology prioritizes safe, continuous operation and often depends on old software. It is frequently connected to other networks, cannot follow laptop patching rules and still needs monitoring.

q: Leaving Bluetooth permanently discoverable on a phone is a safe default.
why: Discoverable mode lets nearby devices find and try to pair with the phone, so it should be used only briefly when pairing.

q: A firewall policy that starts from default deny is generally stronger than one that starts from default allow.
why: Default deny permits only what has been explicitly approved, so the attack surface stays small and unknown traffic is blocked.

q: A device on an air-gapped network can never be infected with malware.
why: Removable media, maintenance laptops and hidden connections can carry malware across an air gap, so isolation reduces but does not remove the risk.

q: Using a cloud provider's service transfers all security responsibility to the provider.
why: Under the shared responsibility model the customer remains responsible for their data, identities and configuration at every service level.

q: A company wants to decide how strongly to protect each of its information stores. What should it do first?
opts: Encrypt everything with the same algorithm
Classify the data by sensitivity and set handling rules
Buy the newest and most expensive security tools available
Move all data to the cloud
why: Classification shows how sensitive each data set is, which drives the strength of controls and handling rules. Treating everything the same wastes effort or leaves sensitive data under-protected, and buying tools or moving to the cloud does not answer what needs protection.

q: A company is retiring old hard drives that held customer records. Which action best ensures the data cannot be recovered?
opts: Deleting the files and then emptying the recycle bin on each PC
Securely destroying the drives by shredding or degaussing
Moving the drives to a storage closet
why: Physical destruction or approved sanitization makes recovery impractical. Deleting and quick formatting leave the data in place and recoverable with common tools, and storing the drives leaves the data fully exposed to anyone who obtains them.

q: A company needs to encrypt a very large database quickly, with both sides already sharing a secret key. Which type of encryption is best suited?
opts: Asymmetric encryption, because it is faster for bulk data
A digital signature, because it hides the content
why: Symmetric encryption is fast and efficient for large amounts of data when a key can be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption is slower and mostly used to exchange keys or sign, hashing cannot be reversed, and signatures prove origin rather than hide content.

q: A forensic analyst copies a suspect's disk and must show a court that the copy is identical to the original. What should the analyst compare?
opts: The file names and folder layout shown on both disks
The hash values of the original and the copy
The time and date shown when the copy was completed
The brand and model of the disk the copy was made onto
why: Identical hash values show that the contents match exactly, as any change would produce a different hash. File names, copy time or disk brand say nothing about whether every bit is the same.

q: A malicious program spreads from computer to computer across a company network by itself, without any user opening a file. What is this type of malware?
why: A worm self-replicates across networks without user action. A trojan pretends to be something useful and needs the user to run it, spyware secretly gathers information, and adware displays unwanted ads.

q: A store's website suddenly receives millions of requests per second from thousands of infected devices and customers cannot load pages. Which attack is this and which property does it target?
opts: On-path attack targeting the integrity of stored data
Phishing, which targets confidentiality of secrets
Brute force guessing, targeting the authentication process
why: A flood from many sources that makes a service unusable is a DDoS attack, which targets availability. On-path attacks intercept traffic, phishing tricks people, and brute force guesses credentials.

q: A company wants one place that collects logs from firewalls, servers and applications, correlates them and alerts on suspicious patterns. Which tool fits?
why: A security information and event management system aggregates and correlates logs and raises alerts. A VPN provides encrypted access, DHCP assigns addresses, and a token is an authentication device.

q: A laptop is confirmed to be infected with malware that is contacting an outside server. Which action is part of the containment phase of incident response?
opts: Isolating the laptop from the network
Reviewing the incident response plan next year
why: Containment limits the spread and damage, and disconnecting the affected system from the network is a typical step. A lessons-learned report is post-incident activity, and plan reviews and purchases are not immediate containment actions.

q: Services are fully restored after a breach and the team meets to discuss what went well, what failed and how to improve. Which phase of the incident response lifecycle is this?
why: Reviewing lessons learned after recovery is post-incident activity. Preparation happens before incidents, detection and analysis happens when an incident is being identified and scoped, and containment limits the damage during the incident.

q: Which two actions help preserve digital evidence for a possible legal case? (Choose two.)
opts: Document everyone who handles the evidence in a chain of custody
Reboot the suspect computer to see what happens
Analyze a verified copy instead of the original media
Delete the malware immediately so it cannot spread
Let each analyst browse the original disk to look for clues
why: A chain of custody shows evidence was handled properly, and working from a verified copy keeps the original unchanged. Rebooting, deleting files or browsing the original media alters or destroys evidence.

q: A hash can be reversed with the right key to recover the original data.
why: Hashing is one-way and uses no key. Encryption is the reversible process that needs a key.

q: Applying vendor patches removes known vulnerabilities, so delaying them leaves systems open to attacks that already exist.
why: Attackers actively exploit known flaws whose fixes are available. Timely, tested patching is one of the most effective risk reductions.

q: If the chain of custody for evidence is broken, the evidence may not be accepted or trusted.
why: Chain of custody shows who held evidence and that it was not altered. Gaps make it possible to argue it was tampered with.

q: A digital signature keeps the content of a message secret from eavesdroppers.
why: A signature proves who signed and that the message was not altered, but it does not hide the content. Encryption provides confidentiality.

q: A developer needs realistic customer data to test an application but must not see real card numbers. Which technique fits best?
opts: Compressing the production database before copying it
Data masking that replaces real values with realistic fake ones
Granting developers administrator rights to production
Hashing the entire production database so that queries run faster
why: Masking supplies realistic but fake values so the real data is not exposed in test. Hashing for speed, production administrator rights and compression either do not hide the data or increase exposure.

q: A shop stops storing real card numbers. Instead it keeps random placeholders, and the real numbers stay in a protected vault at its payment provider. Which technique is this?
why: Replacing a sensitive value with a random token, with the original held in a vault, is tokenization. Degaussing erases magnetic media, port scanning probes services and digital signing proves origin.

q: A contractor treats an unmarked design document as public because nothing on it says otherwise. Which control would most likely have prevented the mistake?
opts: More frequent backups of the document library
Longer passwords for the contractor's account
A stronger firewall at the network edge
Labeling data when it is created
why: A visible label tells people how to handle the data. A firewall, longer passwords and backups do not communicate handling requirements.

q: A company will donate a laptop whose drive supports self-encryption. It needs strong assurance that no data can be recovered. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Cryptographic erase, or another purge method
Delete the user's files and empty the recycle bin
Quick-format the drive and reinstall the system
Rename the data folders to hide their contents
why: Purge techniques, including cryptographic erase for drives that support it, resist recovery even with laboratory methods. Deleting, quick formatting and renaming leave the data in place.

q: Under NIST's media sanitization terms, which level means physically destroying the media, for example by shredding?
why: Destroy renders the media itself unusable. Clear overwrites data with standard tools, purge uses stronger methods that resist laboratory recovery, and archive means keeping the data.

q: Which control best protects customer data while it travels between a branch office and headquarters?
opts: Full-disk encryption on the branch laptops
TLS or an encrypted VPN tunnel
Write blockers on the forensic workstation
why: Data in transit is protected by encrypting the connection with TLS or a VPN. Disk encryption protects data at rest, masking protects test data and write blockers support forensics.

q: A bank must keep some records confidential for 25 years. Why are its architects already planning to adopt quantum-resistant algorithms?
opts: Every TLS certificate in use today has already expired this year
Quantum computers will make every hash function reversible for attackers
Symmetric keys can no longer be used by banks or other regulated firms
Attackers can record data now and decrypt it once quantum computers exist
why: This is the harvest-now, decrypt-later risk: data stolen today could be decrypted in the future, so long-lived secrets need protection against future capability. Hashes are not reversible, symmetric encryption remains usable and certificates have not all expired.

q: Which NIST standard specifies ML-KEM, a quantum-resistant key-establishment mechanism?
why: FIPS 203 specifies the module-lattice-based key-encapsulation mechanism ML-KEM. FIPS 140-3 covers cryptographic module validation, FIPS 197 specifies AES and SP 800-61 concerns incident response.

q: A company stores its database encryption keys in the same folder as the encrypted backups. What is the main weakness?
opts: The backups will compress poorly and take up more storage
Anyone who obtains the backups also obtains the keys
The database will be unavailable during backups
why: Keys kept beside the data they protect defeat the encryption, because one theft yields both. Compression, expiry and availability are unrelated.

q: A company wants to block employees from emailing files that contain card numbers to outside addresses. Which technology fits?
why: Data loss prevention inspects content leaving the organization and applies rules to block or flag it. An IDS alerts on traffic patterns, a load balancer distributes requests and network access control admits devices.

q: During an incident, an analyst posts screenshots containing customer records in a public chat room to ask for help. Which document did the analyst ignore?
why: Incident records and evidence are sensitive data and must follow the data handling policy, including need-to-know sharing. The other documents are not the governing rule here.

q: A security operations center has 500 open alerts. One shows a domain administrator signing in from two continents within five minutes. What should the analyst do?
opts: Escalate it first: privileged account, impossible travel
Handle all 500 alerts strictly in the order they were received
Wait for the weekly report before anyone looks at it again
Close it as a probable false positive because staff travel
why: Privileged accounts and impossible travel point to likely compromise with high impact, so it takes priority in triage. First-in first-out ignores risk, assuming travel dismisses it and waiting for a report both delay response.

q: A monitoring rule raises an alert on a legitimate nightly backup job, treating it as an attack. What is this outcome called?
why: Flagging harmless activity as malicious is a false positive. A false negative misses a real attack, a true positive correctly flags one, and a true negative correctly ignores harmless activity.

q: A SIEM links a failed VPN login, a new-device alert and a large outbound transfer from the same user into one high-priority alert. Which capability is this?
why: Combining events from different sources into one pattern is correlation. Masking hides values, hashing fingerprints data and load balancing spreads traffic.

q: A government-backed group quietly steals designs from defense contractors over several years. Which threat actor type best fits?
why: Well-resourced, long-running espionage backed by a government describes a nation-state actor, often called an advanced persistent threat. Hacktivists act from ideology, script kiddies use ready-made tools and a careless insider causes accidents.

q: A group defaces a company's website to protest its environmental record. What is the most likely motivation?
why: Public protest over a cause is ideological motivation, typical of hacktivists. Nothing in the scenario points to ransom, spying or a personal grievance.

q: A departing employee copies the customer list to a personal drive the day before leaving. Which kind of threat actor is this?
why: A person with legitimate access who misuses it on purpose is a malicious insider. The other actors are outsiders and the scenario involves no cause or foreign government.

q: A threat feed lists IP addresses and file hashes tied to a current ransomware campaign. What type of intelligence is this?
opts: Physical security intelligence about building access
Financial intelligence about company accounts and budgets
Strategic intelligence about long-term industry trends
why: Specific addresses and hashes are technical indicators that tools can match against logs. Strategic intelligence describes broad trends for leaders, and the other categories are not types of cyber threat intelligence.

q: What is the most direct use of a list of indicators of compromise?
opts: Writing the next security awareness newsletter for staff
Choosing the layout and color scheme of the security dashboard
Replacing the entire annual risk assessment process with the list
Searching logs and tools for matches to known threats
why: Indicators are matched against logs, traffic and endpoints to find evidence of known threats. They do not replace risk assessment or serve presentation purposes.

q: A team wants a common vocabulary for attacker techniques and a way to map which of them its detections cover. Which resource fits?
why: MITRE ATT&CK catalogs real-world adversary tactics and techniques so defenders can map detections. The OSI model describes networking layers, PCI DSS covers card data and the Code of Ethics covers professional conduct.

q: An email attachment installs malware that then contacts the attacker's server for instructions. Which two Cyber Kill Chain stages do these steps represent?
why: Installing the malware is the installation stage, and calling out for instructions is command and control. Reconnaissance and weaponization come earlier, and actions on objectives is the final stage.

q: Which four core features describe each intrusion event in the Diamond Model?
why: The Diamond Model relates the adversary, their capability, the infrastructure used and the victim. The other sets describe the security triad with privacy, framework functions and organizational elements.

q: A company tests its incident response plan by having managers talk through a ransomware scenario around a table, without touching live systems. What is this exercise called?
why: A discussion-based walk-through of a made-up incident is a tabletop exercise. Full interruption actually shuts systems down, a penetration test attacks systems and a scan checks for known weaknesses.

q: Which type of incident response exercise has the highest realism and the highest risk to operations?
why: A full-scale exercise uses real systems, teams and communications, so it is the most realistic and the most disruptive. Discussions and reminders do not touch operations.

q: Which factor most directly decides how an incident is escalated?
opts: The length of the alert message
The vendor of the logging tool
The day of the week it was reported
why: Severity based on impact drives who is notified and how fast. Day of the week, message length and tooling vendor do not reflect the harm.

q: During a breach an intern posts updates on social media. Which plan element should have prevented this?
opts: A password complexity rule for staff accounts
A hardware inventory of every laptop and server
A communications plan with named spokespeople
A backup rotation schedule for all of the servers
why: Incident plans specify who may speak, to whom and through which channels, and keep details need-to-know. Backup schedules, inventories and password rules do not control public statements.

q: After a phishing incident, leadership wants to blame the employee who clicked. What is the best way to run the lessons-learned meeting?
opts: Name the employee in the report so that others will take more care
Skip the meeting altogether to save time and effort for the team
Discipline the employee before reviewing any facts
Focus on process gaps and record improvement actions
why: A blameless review finds why controls and processes allowed the incident and produces improvements, and it keeps people willing to report. Naming, skipping and prejudging all weaken learning.

q: Which statement about NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 is accurate?
opts: It aligns incident response with CSF 2.0 and replaced Rev. 2
It defines the requirements of the PCI DSS for card merchants
It was withdrawn by NIST in 2025 and has no replacement document at all
It applies only to cloud service providers and their direct customers
why: Revision 3, published in April 2025, supersedes Revision 2 and maps incident response to the CSF 2.0 functions. It was not withdrawn, is not cloud-specific and has nothing to do with PCI DSS.

q: A hospital still runs a diagnostic workstation on an operating system whose vendor ended security updates years ago. It cannot be replaced this year. What is the best interim action?
opts: Give it a public IP address so the vendor can offer remote support
Isolate it on a restricted segment and add compensating controls
Disable its logging to improve the performance of the workstation
Leave it connected exactly as it is, since it still works fine for staff
why: Unpatchable systems should be isolated, tightly limited and monitored while a replacement is planned. Leaving it exposed, adding a public address or disabling logging raises the risk.

q: An organization cannot say how many cloud workloads it runs or who owns them. What should it do first?
opts: Move everything back on premises to regain control
Buy more security tools to cover the unknown workloads
Build and maintain an inventory with named owners
Write a longer acceptable use policy for cloud services
why: Protection depends on knowing the assets and who is accountable for each. More tools, a move or a longer policy do not tell the organization what it has.

q: Marketing signs up for an unapproved cloud file-sharing service to hold customer lists. What is this called, and what is the best response?
opts: Business continuity; copy more lists into it as an extra backup
Defense in depth; leave it in place because it adds one more useful layer
Tokenization; ignore it because the customer lists are already protected
Shadow IT; find it, assess the risk and offer a secure alternative
why: Unapproved tools used outside IT oversight are shadow IT, and the best response is to find them, assess the risk and offer a secure route. The other pairings do not describe the situation.

q: A change to a production firewall passed testing but caused an outage in production. Which part of change management would have shortened the outage most?
opts: A rollback plan prepared in advance
A new logo and layout for the change request form
A longer change approval meeting with more attendees
A larger change window scheduled late at night
why: A prepared rollback plan lets the team return quickly to the last good state. Longer meetings, bigger windows and form design do not undo a failed change.

q: A scan shows several servers differ from the approved hardened configuration even though no change tickets exist. What is this called?
why: Unplanned departure from the baseline is configuration drift. Privilege creep concerns accumulated access rights, tokenization replaces data values and data exfiltration is theft of data.

q: A company returns leased laptops to the vendor. Which step must happen before the devices leave?
opts: Leave the encryption keys on the machines
Sanitize the storage and update the inventory record
Share the administrator passwords with the vendor
why: Data must be sanitized, and the asset record updated, before the devices leave the organization's control. Handing over passwords or keys and posting serial numbers create new exposure.

q: A manager wants a weekly automated check across all servers for missing patches and known weaknesses. Which activity is this?
why: Automated, broad, routine checks for known weaknesses are vulnerability scans. Red team and penetration tests are targeted attempts to exploit, and a tabletop is a discussion exercise.

q: A company wants proof of whether an attacker could chain several weaknesses to reach its customer database. Which activity gives that?
why: A penetration test actively exploits and chains weaknesses to show real impact. A scan lists possible weaknesses, a policy review reads documents and a backup test checks recoverability.

q: A team wants attackers and defenders to work together in real time so that detection rules improve during the exercise. Which approach fits?
why: Purple teaming pairs red and blue so each attack step is checked against detections and improved immediately. The other options do not combine the two teams in real time.

q: With permission, a group tries to reach executive mailboxes by any realistic path while the monitoring staff are not told when it will happen. What is this?
why: A goal-driven simulation of a real adversary that tests detection and response is a red team exercise. A scan, recovery test and checklist do not simulate an adversary.

q: Developers want to find injection flaws by analyzing source code before the application is deployed or even run. Which technique fits?
why: Static analysis reads code without running it, which catches flaws early. Dynamic testing needs a running application, and physical and tabletop exercises are not code analysis.

q: A security team tests a running web application by sending crafted requests from outside, with no access to the source code. Which technique is this?
why: Testing a running application from outside is dynamic testing. Static testing reads code, a code review needs the source and threat modeling is a design activity.

q: During design, a team asks what can go wrong with an application and sorts the answers into spoofing, tampering and information disclosure. Which technique is this?
why: Asking what can go wrong and categorizing threats with STRIDE is threat modeling, done during design. The other activities test production or people, not the design.

q: A tester in a delivery uniform follows staff through a secured door and photographs unattended screens. What is being tested?
opts: Firewall rules on the perimeter gateway
Wireless encryption on the guest network
Backup integrity of the file server data
why: Tailgating and impersonation test physical access control and employee behavior. Firewall rules, backups and wireless encryption are not involved, and a legitimate test needs written authorization.

q: Before a penetration test begins, which document defines which systems may be tested and when?
opts: The acceptable use policy for company laptops
The disaster recovery plan for the data center
The risk register maintained by management
Rules of engagement and scope agreement
why: Rules of engagement set scope, timing, techniques and contacts, and protect both parties. The other documents do not authorize or bound a test.

q: A scanner reports 400 findings. Which approach best prioritizes remediation?
opts: Combine severity with asset importance and exploitation
Fix them in alphabetical order by product name
Wait until attackers actually exploit one before acting on any
Fix the easiest ones first, whatever their importance may be
why: Prioritizing by severity, business importance and evidence of exploitation focuses effort where risk is highest. Alphabetical or easiest-first ordering ignores risk, and waiting invites attack.

q: Which two statements about vulnerability scans and penetration tests are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A scan is automated and finds known weaknesses broadly
A penetration test tries to exploit weaknesses under agreed rules
A scan always exploits the weaknesses it finds
A penetration test needs no authorization
why: Scans are automated and broad, while penetration tests are authorized attempts to exploit. A scan does not exploit, tests require written authorization and the two are different activities.

q: Which two techniques help protect sensitive data in test environments? (Choose two.)
opts: Copying production data to developers' laptops
why: Masked or synthetic data gives realistic testing without exposing the real thing. Copying production data, broad rights and no logging all increase exposure.

q: Which two are indicators of compromise? (Choose two.)
opts: A connection to a known malicious IP address
A file whose hash matches known ransomware
why: Known bad addresses and file hashes are classic indicators. Maintenance windows, first logins and budget reports are normal business activity.

q: Which two activities belong to post-incident activity? (Choose two.)
opts: Updating plans and controls based on the findings
Spotting the first signs of the compromise
Writing the first alert rule for an unknown threat
why: After recovery the team reviews what happened and improves plans and controls. Isolation is containment and spotting the first signs is detection and analysis.

q: Which two are risks of keeping software past its end of support? (Choose two.)
opts: No security patches for newly found flaws
Vendors and insurers may no longer back it
why: Without vendor fixes, new vulnerabilities stay open, and support and insurance may be withdrawn. Software past support does not gain encryption, compatibility or patches.

q: Tokenization replaces a sensitive value with a random placeholder, while the original is kept in a protected vault.
why: The token has no mathematical relationship to the original, so stealing tokens alone reveals nothing. Only the vault can map a token back.

q: Post-quantum cryptography algorithms are designed to resist attacks from large quantum computers.
why: NIST's FIPS 203, 204 and 205 specify algorithms intended to remain secure even against quantum computers that could break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.

q: A false positive is a real attack that monitoring fails to detect.
why: That is a false negative. A false positive is harmless activity wrongly flagged as an attack.

q: A tabletop exercise requires taking production systems offline.
why: A tabletop is a discussion-based walk-through of a scenario and does not touch production systems.

q: A vulnerability scan proves that each reported weakness can actually be exploited.
why: Scans report possible weaknesses and can include false positives. Penetration testing is what demonstrates exploitability.

q: A penetration tester may start testing a client without written authorization as long as the client is a friendly company.
why: Written authorization and rules of engagement are required before testing, since unauthorized access can be illegal whoever the target is.

q: Software that has reached end of support continues to receive routine security patches from the vendor.
why: End of support means the vendor stops providing security fixes, so newly found vulnerabilities remain unpatched.

q: In purple teaming, the red and blue teams share findings with each other during the exercise.
why: Purple teaming is collaborative: attacks and detections are discussed in real time so defenses improve immediately.

q: Shadow IT is a concern only when the unapproved tool is free.
why: Cost is irrelevant. Any tool used outside IT's knowledge is outside inventory, patching, monitoring and data handling rules.
